churn_resistance.rationale: The single data-access module and one-file config are genuinely churn-resistant, but the complete absence of types at the data boundaries (the app's biggest risk surface), copy-pasted not-found wiring across four routes, and re-implementing router-provided search-param handling mean refactors and framework upgrades will ripple more than they should.

findings.issue: The whole app is untyped JavaScript, including a ~450-line module that reshapes deeply nested third-party API payloads (pokemon stats, moves, evolution chains) with optional chaining everywhere; a field rename or shape change in the API fails silently at render time.
findings.suggestion: Convert at least lib/data.js and its return values to TypeScript (tsconfig is already strict); the framework's templates and docs are TS-first, and typed query return values would catch contract drift at build time.

findings.issue: apiFetch caches the in-flight promise including its null result on fetch failure, so a single transient API error permanently serves 'Not found' pages until the server process restarts.
findings.suggestion: Only cache successful resolutions (or cache {data} with a short TTL for failures), so the in-memory cache can't poison a live-data view.

findings.issue: updateParams and pageHref hand-build query strings with URLSearchParams and navigate(); the router's setSearchParams already merges values and deletes null/undefined/empty keys, preserving the hash and defaulting scroll behavior.
findings.suggestion: Use the [params, setParams] = useSearchParams() setter with { replace: true } for the filters and page links, reducing duplicated URL-shaping logic that could drift from router behavior.

findings.issue: The <Show when={data() === null}>NotFound</Show> / <Show when={data()}>Content</Show> pair is duplicated in all four detail routes.
findings.suggestion: Extract a small <DetailPage query={...} params={...}>{data => ...}</DetailPage> helper so 404 wiring lives in one place.

findings.issue: The debounce timer is stored in a component-scope let and never cleared on disposal, so a pending navigation can fire after the route unmounts.
findings.suggestion: Wrap in createDisposable/onCleanup(() => clearTimeout(searchTimer)) or own it in a signal.

findings.issue: Hash scrolling to #moves is a one-shot onMount reading window.location.hash directly; it doesn't re-run if the user navigates within the same route with a different hash.
findings.suggestion: Derive from the reactive useLocation().hash (createEffect) or rely on the router's scroll/anchor handling so the behaviour tracks the framework.

findings.issue: nitro is pinned to a pre-release RC channel (3.0.261029-rc); until nitro v3 stable ships, every RC bump is a potential rebuild-behaviour change.
findings.suggestion: Fine for today (this is what SolidStart v2 requires), but watch for the v3 stable release and pin against it when it lands.

findings.issue: The home query fans out one pokemon/<id> fetch per card (48 per page) on top of the species index; fine while the promise cache is warm, but the first request of every filter combination is an N-way burst.
findings.suggestion: Consider a single cached per-pokemon-shape lookup keyed once, or server-side pagination of the type/generation joins, so list-page cost doesn't scale with API round-trips.

summary: This is a current-generation SolidStart app: SolidStart v2 stable (Aug 2026) on Vite 8 + Nitro v3, server queries with "use server", route preload, FileRoutes and HttpStatusCode all used exactly as the v2 docs prescribe, with zero legacy-era APIs and no dependency bloat. What will age less well is the surrounding code quality rather than the framework usage: the app is entirely untyped including a large API-shaping data layer, permanently caches failed fetches, and re-implements search-param handling the router already provides. I'd merge it after the fetch-failure caching and the hand-rolled URL handling are addressed, with types flagged as fast follow-up.
